posts.author: tpark
posts.post_subject: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.content_md:
Hi,

I have some questions about laser diode systems suitable for making holograms. I purchased and built that driver system from D&S lasers, and so far I've had good results with the Panasonic LNCQ05PS device, however I did have some sliced bread holograms with the ML1016R diode. That could be due to insufficient goop (heat sink compound) on the back of the diode, causing overheating, which is a Bad Thing. 

1) What other diodes have people had good luck with?

2) Does anyone have a PDF for the IR3C07 device? I looked at the old

 archives, but that link is no longer active. Also, is there a source

 or replacement for this item? I'd like to be able to play with the

 current drive, to see if I can look for mode hops that way. 

3) Has anyone tried cooling one of those green laser pointer diode modules

 in an attempt to get the module to be stable enough for holography?

Here's my results so far:

Device 					Results

------------------------------------------------------

Intergraf laser module			Good results

25mw ebay laser module			Sliced bread

15mw 635nm ebay laser module		Sliced bread

15mw HeNe ebay laser			Good results

Diode from cheap pointer		Good results

D&S driver driving ML1016R		Mixed - 1 good ref, 4 bad transmission

module from green ebay laser ptr	sliced bread

D&S driver driving LNCQ05PS		Good results for 2 transmission

Thanks for any help you can provide on this. This forum has been

a great help, especially for a amateur newbie like me.

posts.content_md:
> **tpark:** 3) Has anyone tried cooling one of those green laser pointer diode modules in an attempt to get the module to be stable enough for holography?

Yes. I carefully "vise-gripped" the pointer to a small block of aluminum, gripping it a little in front of the power switch. I setup a Michellson and saw that it took more than 45 minutes for the fringes to settle down, but they did. Use really fresh batteries.

I shot a single 4x5 Denisyuk on VRP film and got something decent. It was dim, but clean. I want to try that again soon. My green pointer is outputing close to 7.5mW. Colin noted previously that after a while the output power on his would drop, rendering it unsusable.

posts.content_md:
> **tpark:** Does anyone have a PDF for the IR3C07 device?

[http://www.designerinlight.com/holo/ir3c07.pdf](http://www.designerinlight.com/holo/ir3c07.pdf)

This link should work. If not let me know. It is not the datasheet but a datasheet from a laser book. It will give you an idea. Try using the original diode but change the value of R5+R6 to change the ratio of output power to the photodiode current. It could be that the D&S circuit only works when the output power is correct and since the diode has a wide range of values for the photodiode current it fails on some diodes. There are reports of D & S circuits being problem free. (Mine makes sliced bread.) Also make sure to use about 9V of DC power from batteries.

posts.topic_title: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.author: tpark
posts.post_subject: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.content_md:
First, thanks for the links and information on the IR3C07 - this is very helpful.

Green laser pointers:

I haven't found a mar-free way of removing the laser diode assembly from the green laser pointer - what I did was grab the end of the thing with a pair of vice grip pliers and carefully wiggle the assembly out. There was some cosmetic damage to the end piece which was pressure fit into the pointer, but overall no actual damage to the diode assembly or the rest of the pointer case. With various tricks like cooling and reducing the drive current, I haven't been able to get the green pointer laser diode assembly to generate a beam stable enough for good holograms. I made another Denisyuk with it, and it showed the sliced bread pattern. The fringes on the interferometer can be made stable, but there are zones where the fringes are fainter, suggesting that perhaps there are other frequencies happening there. The beam has a gaussian distribution, but even so, there have to be other bad things happening in there.

I might try using a TEC cooling assembly bolted to an aluminium block

with a laser module sized hole drilled in it, but it looks like the green lasers aren't suitable for holography regardless of what adjustments/cooling tricks are done. 

D&S driver/diode combination:

When I purchased the diodes from Optima Optics, I also purchased their laser diode holder. This is a fairly large (as far as laser assemblies go) assembly that looks like it could act as a good heat sink. This could be a factor in getting stable operation.

When I assembled the driver, I was careful to keep path lengths short,

and the leads to the diode are quite short, however these things might

not be enough to reduce RF interference.

I'll try the original ML1016R diode again once I get the second mounting assembly. 

I think here's my next course of action:

1) Use lots of goop this time on the diode.

2) add a potentiometer to change Raj, and use a laser power meter to set the drive current. I suspect that diode/photosensor assemblies aren't a "one size fits all" situation - other drivers I've seen have adjustments for drive current.

3) add a 4700pf capacitor between pins 3 and 7 of the device - according to that PDF data sheet, this may be required to prevent oscillations.

4) shield/bypass the electronics. This will also give me the opportunity to mount the voltage regulator to the case as well.

> **Tom B.:** tpark wrote:Hi,Device 					Results------------------------------------------------------Intergraf laser module			Good results25mw ebay laser module			Sliced bread15mw 635nm ebay laser module		Sliced bread15mw HeNe ebay laser			Good resultsDiode from cheap pointer		Good resultsD&S driver driving ML1016R		Mixed - 1 good ref, 4 bad transmissionmodule from green ebay laser ptr	sliced breadD&S driver driving LNCQ05PS		Good results for 2 transmissionMy results:Intergraf laser module			Good results, but faint vertical stripes25mw Midwest laser module	 Sliced breadDiode from cheap pointer	 Very good results, no stripesresistor limited ML1016R		Some sliced bread, less at lower powerresistor limited Sanyo DL3148 635nm Good results, but tricky to stabilizeresitor limited LNCQ05PS		Very good results. My workhorseI suspect that the sliced bread (multimode behavior) of some ML1016s is inherent to the diode and will not be reduced by improving the driver, but I could be wrong.

But then again, you could be right. It seems as though there's some correllation between fancy power control, and multimode behavior though. Having said that, if you get bad results with a resistor/diode combination, the device itself may be the problem. I think some more

testing is in order.

I have done some further tests over the weekend.

I did get a sliced bread hologram with my D&S driver/LNCQ05PS - the problem may have been due to insufficient warm up, and the diode being too close to the shutter card (when I lift the card, it could have created a draft around the diode, causing a mode hop). A later image where I had let the diode warm up for 45 minutes, and had it placed further away from the card appears to be OK. 

I'm starting to wonder if the optical feedback system which controls laser

diode current from the photodiode causes problems with mode stability - rather than applying constant current, it's possible that some hunting is possible in such a system. I note that the resistor limited systems seem to give the best results. I wonder if it's due to better **current** stability rather than better power stability. If the power is kept constant, the current could be moving around somewhat, and that may be what is causing the mode hops.

--Ted

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.post_subject: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.content_md:
> **tpark:** I'm starting to wonder if the optical feedback system which controls laserdiode current from the photodiode causes problems with mode stability - rather than applying constant current, it's possible that some hunting is possible in such a system.--Ted

I prefer constant-current drive to APC for this reason. With APC, the drive current is sensitive to back-reflections into the laser and photodiode, one of the most problematic reflections being from the shutter. Open the shutter, less light reflects back, and the APC increases the drive current to compensate - just what you don't want to happen during an exposure.

I think I may have noticed some sliced bread with the LNCQ05 running at higher output power - around 40 mW versus the 30 mW I normally run at. I had noticed something similar wiith the ML1016 (worse behavior at higher power). Conventional laser diode wisdom has it that mode purity should INCREASE with output power, so I dunno what's going on.

posts.topic_title: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.post_subject: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.content_md:
> Open the shutter, less light reflects back, and the APC increases the drive current to compensate - just what you don't want to happen during an exposure.

I place my shutter after a very small transfer mirror to help with this. I also place the shutter at an angle to the beam.

> Conventional laser diode wisdom has it that mode purity should INCREASE with output power, so I dunno what's going on.

My theory about this is that the diode is more porne to mode hops when it is having to disipate more heat. When it is running lower power the heat is easier to disipate. I think if we were to use a spectrum analyser we would find that the instantianous mode purity does indeed improve with increasing current. I can't find the paper that talks about mode purity and output power but Tom refered me to it origionally.

posts.topic_title: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.author: Tom B.
posts.post_subject: Medium power laser diodes for use with holography.
posts.content_md: I can see how there would be a larger thermal gradient between the diode junction and the ambient when running at higher power - maybe it would have some minor stability effects like convection currents etc. But I think what I'm seeing is not so much mode hopping (rapid dithering between adjacent modes), but weak secondary modes operating simultaneously with the main mode. Maybe for some diodes the gain profile of the cavity flattens out at higher current density, making it less selective and letting the weaker modes through... or some such thing.

I also place the shutter at an angle to the beam.Conventional laser diode wisdom has it that mode purity should INCREASE with output power, so I dunno what's going on.My theory about this is that the diode is more porne to mode hops when it is having to disipate more heat. When it is running lower power the heat is easier to disipate. I think if we were to use a spectrum analyser we would find that the instantianous mode purity does indeed improve with increasing current. I can't find the paper that talks about mode purity and output power but Tom refered me to it origionally.

The transfer mirror idea seems like something that would help - I too place the card at an angle. I'm using a blackened card, which is bent and taped with a piece of duct tape so it can stand on its own. My experience has been that if the card is too close to the diode assembly, sliced bread holograms result. The Intergraf diode seems less prone to this, but my cheapo pointer diode and the LNCQ05PS assembly both seem prone to this problem. I built a draft shield assembly for around the diode, and that seems to help.

Tom B.'s comments seem about right to me too.

If the laser is being driven at higher power, there would be a greater temperature difference between the device and the surrounding air. Perhaps convection around the device becomes more of a problem as the diode heats up. I wonder if mounting the diode in a big copper temperature controlled block would help. I don't know much about the detailed physics of laser diodes, so I really can't comment on how the temperature changes affect the mode behavior of the diode.

I'm using the Optima optical bench mount kit, which has a rather

large mass compared to other diode holders. This seems to work pretty good overall, but again, I did get sliced bread holograms when I had the card too close to the diode assembly.

I've obtained some constant current driver boards, and I'll do some experiments with those. I have a 50mw Hitachi diode which I got from Ebay, so I can do some preliminary trials with that, rather than baking my new diodes. Running constant current at powers well below the diodes maximum seems like a good strategy.
